blocks.x: All right, ready to go. This is August 28th, 1963 in the Tulane Jazz Archive. Is that correct? Paul Crawford and Ed Kahn interviewing Naki Parker. Let's start at the beginning and get

where you were from, when you were born, and your real name. John Parker, 1918, August the 8th, Palmer, Texas. And were your parents musically inclined? No, we had a cotton farm out there and a player piano that I was interested in all my life and that's about how I got started.
You want to go into more detail on the early music?

We used to have itinerant musicians who'd come through there and from the beginning I'd learned how to play by copying the notes going down on the player piano. Put a roll in and see the notes going down and then make the same notes go down in the same combinations. Children have keenly, keen sensitivities and can watch things going on and can absorb more being children somehow than we as adults can. Innovations of immortality and all that. And as a child you can see keenly little patterns going down, patterns of notes and clusters and then make the same combinations. One, three, five is easy for a child to see uncluttered by our own activities and other fields and copy the same things and play just like the phonograph, just like the player piano roll did. From then we had an old sonora phonograph and I could get records for the phonograph and copy them much the same way by ear because I'd already had the authority of learning from the player piano rolls first. And that's how I started playing the piano, by copying the rolls and the records that I heard. And that's been, I guess, with me all my life. How old were you when you started copying the rolls? I was four. Mama was on the phone one time and she heard something, she heard something but she knew this wasn't exactly the roll because it wasn't quite as full as that but still sort of like that it came in and I was playing the piano, the same little piece that we had on the roll. What was the piece? I don't know. I think, I know one of these first things was Jesus lover of my soul and another thing was aggravating Papa. The old thing there I always liked Russell. Russell Robinson's playing in 1920, aggravating Papa came out and I remember that's one of the tunes
that I used to like mainly. What generally were the kind of roles that you had around the house?

Oh, we had old Hilo March and all those that were popular at the time. And, but I do remember that thing by Russell Robinson. And I was surprised to visit Trevor Titchener in St. Louis to see some, some beautiful Creole bells, a cakewalk. And that was one of the ones he put this on and I remembered that years ago this is an old tune that I had particularly liked and had played many, many times. We had old, all the old carry mills things and pieces like Snow Deer, Rufus on Parade, all the old cakewalks and early rags.
When was it then that you got the phonograph and started listening to the records?

Les, I don't know all this because before the, before I went to school. Between the period there from when I was four to six primarily was filled with musical activity. As soon as I started playing, they would carry me around to camp meetings in the summer. And have, so, so, you're going to play florid arpeggio versions of old, those two page hymns, Awakening Chorus and All Hail Emmanuel. The hymns in the Protestant hymn book there with many razzle dazzle scale pages up and down the keyboard from four and five year old, you know, they liked that back in the country days, in the old times in Texas.
You got the phonograph record right after you started playing the piano roll.
Yes, right, right in that same period there. These are influences that came on me when I was a kid.
Yeah. And what kind of records was your family buying?

Well, there was a Miss Hazel Booth at Whittle's Music Company who would put aside all through the year all piano solos that would come in. We had, I remember, things by Kalkia Davenport and old Jelly Roll, lots of Jelly Roll Martin pieces and Clarence Williams, early Wildflower Rag and Argan Grindr Blues and Kansas City Stomp by Jelly, Seattle Hunch. And in the fall, when Daddy would sell cotton and all, we had money, we'd go to Dallas quite frequently. And then we'd go by there, buy all those records that she had put aside all through the year waiting for me to come up.
It was mainly piano music that they liked.
Oh yeah. I was always, you know, it was all.
Were they buying them for you or for them?
Oh no, these were mine. These were for you? This was a kid always at home, you know, they were, and they would have just, before I could talk, even they'd bring home player roles and give it to me.
How did their own musical tastes run?

Oh, I don't think they really had much of, they weren't primarily interested in that. They were familiar, they liked what I liked, and they got what was coming out to the whole market, all kinds of pieces.
Did you hear any live musicians during this time?

Yes. We'd go to Dallas in the fall to get these cotton pickers, seasonal interest. And in the plus years of the twenties, it was hard to get labor. And Daddy would go there searching for musicians to come work in the cotton fields. And I'd go up there with him. And we'd go over there in deep Ellum, two syllables, the L-M. They had this deep Ellum special, the switchblade knife that would come out. And I didn't know anything about it. I was just a kid going there with Daddy. And he'd go to all kinds of places. Sometimes some of the places he'd go to would have a piano and I'd start playing. I don't know how it got started, but at any rate, they'd call up all other people around. At these Negro, all kinds of sometimes disreputable places in degree at least. And people would come there with their homemade instruments and a lot of guitarists, especially many, many guitarists, I remember, would come there. And we'd play together. And the pianists, too, would sit down, you know, play four hands on the piano and then shift your hand so that it'd be my left hand, his left hand, my right hand, his right, and move all over the piano, playing all kinds of ways and variations. And I'd try to copy everything they did, you see. And they liked this very much. And would laugh and show me everything they played. And this is how then I learned from them. They were my first teachers. Terrific musicians, really.
These were Negroes and whites?

Well, Negroes. All of these were Negroes there in Dallas. Yes, down there in that Negro section there. They got to where they looked forward to my coming up there. And they'd all get on the phone and call up. And they'd all come over there. We'd have little jam sessions, little substandard instrumentation, I'm sure. Anything they'd have, they'd bring up. French harp. Very much like that Sleepy John Estes deal, you know. The harmonica, whether you... Hammer and Nixon, is it? Anyway, all kinds of players. Any of them who would come around. Blind Lemon was one, I met one time there. I remember. Just barely do remember it. And Will Ezell was there on one occasion, at least. I remember this one time. And some of these musicians really played extraordinarily well. They had kind of a style of their own that was peculiar. They used to drink... Oh, I don't know. Every time they'd get something to drink with themselves, they'd get me a Dixie cup. Those were just coming into popularity in the 20s. Dixie cups. And on the piano there would be all the bottles there, the Dixie cups, all lined up there on top of the piano. And then we'd stay over there for all hours. Your father would just sit around and listen to this? Oh, yes. He loved it going there. It was sort of a greed that I was not supposed to tell the other people exactly what sort of places we went to. They suspected. But Daddy liked going along there, you know, and having me up there. He thought, this is great, of course. And the music was great. And I was getting the finest training that you could possibly get anywhere from all these wild people.
The main instruments were piano and guitar.
Guitar, yes. And sometimes that lap string bass on a washtub. Sometimes two strings they would play sometimes.
What did they call that instrument?
I don't know. But Crawford, what?
They call it here, they call it a tub of form.
I never did hear, I don't know what the, uh, washtub bass is what I think I used to hear, but I'm not sure.
Yeah.
And they'd have two strings sometimes.
Two strings? How would they be attached?
I don't know, but they would have two strings there. He'd play first one, then the other, leaning it over to get, uh, tension, to get, uh, the right notes and all.
Mm-hmm. Gee. This was the first time you had heard a bass used in this kind of music.
Yes. I hadn't heard anything used in this kind of music before. It got a big kick out of going up there with him.
And would all these, would this be an ensemble group of guitars and piano and bass and French art?

Just anybody who would come in would sit down there and play, and we'd play a while, and they'd all laugh and talk around, and they'd make fun. But, uh, very, it was, uh, not satire. They would just make, uh, pleasant fun, you know, of all the pianists, but they'd still show me all their stuff because I was just a kid, and of course they saw that I liked them, and there was never any feeling of black and white at all, never involved, which was kind of strange. And sometimes I'd stay behind the bar in the back room or somewhere and go to sleep, while Daddy would go off doing some kind of business or work or something. And at one time, when there was some kind of a fight, some of the people would hustle me out of there, and they sort of took care of me. It wasn't between five and, uh, it stopped about 1928, I guess. Uh, five, between five and ten, five, six, seven, eight, nine.
Just a young kid.
Yeah, you know that.
How would you characterize the music they were playing?

Oh, it was very much like, uh, those, uh, very close to, uh, the later Chicago Barrel House idiom, close to that sort of thing. Close to, uh, fundamental boogie-woogie, not, not in the, uh, complicated forms of Pine Top, but earlier, like the Cow-Cow School, very much like that. A lot of times they would get on one note and repeat it for a long time, up high or low, either one, a whole lot of that.
Jimmy Yancey or back there?

Closer to Yancey, yes, than before. Even before. Yancey and, uh, oh, uh, who was that other one? Not Cow-Cow, who came before. We had, uh, the, uh, Railroad Express, that old fellow who created Walking Base before Yancey. I'll think of the name in just a minute, I know. Railroad Express. Lorenzo. Cripple Clarence Lofton. Yeah, sure. Cripple Clarence, of course.
Pretty much that style.
Yeah, kind of, uh, stripped.
Mm-hmm. Just the real outline.
Yes, bare, bare.
And then the guitar would fit in with this. Now, how would you characterize the guitar style?

Uh, very much like, uh, Blind Lemon, and, uh, in a way, Lead Belly. Although I don't remember the 12th string, I don't think. I don't remember it. It might have been there. And there was somebody who would lead, uh, he did it unentrusively, so that you scarcely noticed it, Blind Lemon around, but I don't remember who that was at all, or have any idea. I know there was somebody there, but this is all very vague in my mind. I don't recall. The guitarist would play kind of a wandering, very freestyle, with a, not entirely, not just plain chord accompaniment, but a kind of a free rolling little, with a lot of little filigrees thrown in every now and then. And not a straightforward chord accompaniment by any means at all.
Hmm. This, uh, you indicated, ended by the time you were about 10.

I don't remember. After the Depression, it was easier, and we didn't go there anymore much. And by that time, I was getting on out and other aspects. And that's, yes, that's about the time it ended, about 28.
Uh, can you carry your life forward a little bit from, as you were going to school at this time?

Um, and... Yes, I joined the, uh, little hillbilly band, Blackie Simmons. And Blackie Simmons saw Duke Ellington's bus pass by one time. They said, Duke Ellington's famous bus. Famous, Duke Ellington's famous orchestra. That's a famous orchestra all outside of the bus. And he had had Blackie's blue jackets, which was, uh, perfectly, uh, illiterative, you see, and, uh, proper title. And then he put Blackie's famous blue jackets, in imitation of Duke Ellington's famous orchestra, on the back of the bus. Blackie used to go out on trips. We'd play little old honky-tonks. They'd not do me honky-tonk. I wasn't in the 16th then. We used to play such things as bathing suit dances in cheap dives. I said, brother, when you play a bathing suit dance in a cheap dive, you've got something indeed. We'd play, uh, all these one-nighters there, and divide up the proceeds. Blackie would get two cuts. He was a leader. His wife took up tickets at the door. She'd get one cut. And, uh, his brother drove the car. He'd get one cut. And then we took out all the mileage for gasoline, and then the boys got one cut apiece. And we'd make then from, oh, by the time we'd total up, this is in lean depression days, from, uh, at least, oh, $8 a week on to sometimes as much as $25 or $30. That was life in the 30s. Were you going to school during this time? That was one year I worked with him. I quit school. Uh, well, no, right after I got out of high school, as soon as I got a, as soon as that degree, I had to, I'm tied down at home until I get out of high school. And the minute June comes around, I graduate from Palmer Senior High. I'm off at once. Just right off that same month, got the job with Blackie Simmons. This stayed on for, uh, half a year. stuff

I went on to school for a half a year, joined them again in the summer, and came back to school for a half a year, then joined the La Crosse Doe Boys, which was a much better style band playing the same tunes with the same instrumentation.
What year was it that you graduated high school?
1935, was it 35? I guess, yeah, 1935. Then I worked with Blackie Simmons for 35 that summer, and a half of a year, and then in the summer of 36, and then I joined the Doe Boys in 36.
Now, we've got from 1928 to 1935, what was your musical activity during this time? That would have been grade school and high school.

Now, I stayed on copying the player piano, no, copying the phonograph rolls that were coming at that time. The phonograph displaced the player piano, and it was easier to get records and wider assortment and study them, and everybody else was having photograph records, and I had them too. The piano receded to them in the background.
And you weren't seeing too many or playing with too many musicians?
No, not so much then. I was getting in upper grammar school and high school then, and was concerned with other work.
What was the first professional job that you had?

I guess as soon as I left high school and joined Blackie Simmons when I was 16. They advertised me as a 12-year-old piano player because I was real small and green, green as a gourd and inexperience. And they got a big kick out of these improper places we played because I was so naive and country. And when the folks found out how terrible the business all was, they jerked me out of there. That was the only reason that we were so, at this time the depression was still going on, and they couldn't afford to stay me to college until they found out how disreputable were my surroundings. Then they could and did. But I got out of college as soon as they joined the Doe Boys.
When did you get out of college?

Well, I quit college there in 19... I had 36 then to join the Doe Boys. I'd been there one year. The last semester of the freshman year, the first semester there of the next year. Then I joined them at once. I went up Christmas during our vacation to have an audition and play on the radio program with them somehow. They had a big radio program all over Texas and Oklahoma. And Eddie Dunn, the announcer, kept saying during this week, even though they were featured pianos, but I don't know how the people could have been, how they would have accepted. He kept saying, seems to be I heard of pianos. Somebody said, oh no, that's just a banjo player. He sounds like that sometimes. And the audience did everything and didn't know any better. And I worked with them a week and then left. And then joined them permanently the next January. As soon as the semester was over in college. But a while at the time when I was working with them as a Doe Boy, I went to night school at TCU and that's how that all came about.
So you were going to college. You were kind of working your way through college playing with the Doe Boys.
That's right, yeah.
Can you tell me the circumstance of how you joined this first band, Blackie Simmons?

Well, I had been playing a few radio programs and dance jobs with Bill Boyd's Cowboy Ramblers. And he had already made arrangements to hire the pianist from Blackie Simmons, but liked my work better. I've forgotten Sonny somebody. He's that first one who made the first records with Bill Boyd. But he'd already made a commitment. And so whenever Blackie's pianist worked with him, I went over to take his place just automatically there. It was catch as catch can in those days, and as it is now, and sometimes it's awfully hard, even in big cities, much less small ones, to get fill-ins. You find that even in your audience, I guess. Is that true? Yeah.
Then you'd been playing with Bill Boyd before you joined Blackie Simmons.
Radio programs and just a few odd jobs scattered around.
Was Bill Boyd the first band you'd played with?
I believe so, yes.
How did this come about? I mean, he was well known.

Yes, I went up there one day and started, went in there, and I don't know how. Somebody told me I played a little piano, and some friend carried me in and introduced me, gave me a build-up, and had me sit in with her for a few numbers, and they liked the way I played and laughed, and I was so little. Even when I graduated from school, I was about old, not old. I don't know how tall, but very, very short enough to get by as being 12 years old. Country, country, country. Grice and hay all over me.
How about the rest of the guys in the band?

Well, they were always good, too. They thought we looked kind of as, you know, kind of a kid or mascot or something in life, but they liked my playing very much, especially the blues. They liked that because that's been my heritage, you see. When we played the blues, I was on home ground.
Well, now, you said that you were a country at that time. How about the rest of the fellows, were they?

Yes, they were a country, too, but they'd been out in, they were from, when we say country, now let's qualify this. It has good aspects as well as unfavorable connotations. But my school, I'd come from a very sheltered background, and some of these musicians I worked with were from Crossford Railroad tracks, and they enjoyed just that much more of my naivety.
So they put you on?

Yeah, always. You can imagine what it would be like. Brother, in those days, when you say you put a ball in that surrounding, man, that was really it. That would be too hard. Tate would have to be made in asbestos to take some of those things that would happen.
Well, I think the Tate could take us. How's it happen that you joined a band like Bill Boyd? I mean, you were a musician.

Well, that was the band that was playing there, and they liked all the, oh, that's what they mainly liked, and whenever we'd play old St. Louis blues and some little old dive there, and I'd take three or four courses, people would come around there, they'd stand around, you see, and they would stop the kind of whole show and take two or three more courses and play the thing. In those days, we would play one tune and stop for a few seconds and then play the same tune again because their repertoire was limited, and we'd play one tune twice, once right after the other. And they'd wait for the courses to come up again and just stand around and watch, and the guitarist was terrific, too. Oh, he was a knockout old Jim Boyd. Played very well, very, very well. And they'd wait for these, for the soloists they'd like, especially the crowd around there, and they'd have a ball. How large a band was this? Oh, there were about two guitars, one of them was a solo and no one of the accompaniments, bass, two violins, banjo, piano. What kind of banjo was that? Now, I don't remember the banjos with Bill Boyd. I don't remember him at all. The banjos that I remember primarily is Marvin Montgomery, the Larkless Dole Boys, who was one of the greatest, oh, banjo pickers of all time, anywhere.
There was a tenor banjo.
Yes, that's right.
Did you make records with Bill Boyd?
Yes.
That was before you had, before you had joined Blackie Simmons.

No, wait a minute. When I was with Bill Boyd, there were just a few odd dancers, and I'd go up there and play with him on the radio program for about a week. When I first went there to Dallas, just before joining over, moving over, and taking the pianist's place, for whom Bill Boyd had already contracted, before I appeared on the scene. During his two weeks' notice, I appeared up there and played with Bill Boyd. Then you switched with him.
And then you came back with Bill Boyd.
Much later on for record dates, yes.
Was that before joining the Larkless Dole Boys?
No, after joining the Dole Boys. After that. Yes.
If in these early times you could have joined any band in the country, what band would you have joined? You know, who was your idol at this time in terms of a band?

Well, bands, I didn't know anything about it. All we had the radio program at home, and our knowledge was very limited. We didn't have anything but just what we heard there. And locally, I guess, over the Larkless Dole Boys was about to appear. They were regarded as the tops in the hillbilly field all up and down the country. Well, this is interesting.

All of the musical description you've given me, this is the first time that you've discussed hillbilly. That is, your life has been with Negro musicians and listening to records up until some point, and then you start playing with hillbilly groups. How did this happen?
That was the only... Those were the only jobs available there for a poor white boy who couldn't read music but could play.
How do you account for the fact that they were playing music so similar to the kind of music you knew?

Well, back there in those days, the guitar was sort of the heart of the hillbilly orchestra, I guess you'd call it a hillbilly band. And the guitar always played strong, strong blues techniques. You see, I had singled out when I talked about St. Louis Blues, the guitar and the piano. We were the ones who would carry those with our old choruses, on and on and on, either fast or slow. Old St. Louis Blues, we'd first play slow tempo, and then fast, and then we'd stop for two or three seconds and play the same thing again. And each time, we'd have long solos in the middle of both slow and fast. And the people would come up there, you see, and holler after each display, very much the way Benny Goodman later on, the people applauding each chorus.
Do you think that these bands at that time were more nearly hillbilly or swing?

Well, not swing yet, because swing hasn't come up. Swing didn't come up until, oh, I guess 36 it was coming, and I joined them in 35, just about. Swing was just beginning to come in. You were, to take this business about swing, the only difference in swing and jazz is simply voicing and prearranged, somehow or other. We see jazz, so to speak, because it's all prearranged and voiced. Voicing, not collective improvisation. And when it becomes a collective improvisation, you're getting back then into jazz. But whenever you start voicing and make pre-planned arrangements, you're getting into swing. Now, in this hillbilly band, you had the two violins playing primarily western. This is the first time we've mentioned the word western. It's very popular here, too, because this is close to the Mexican settlements there in Dallas and Fort Worth. And we used to play all Yara Rancho Grande, Capulita de Alili, a whole lot of, all kinds of, and all the La Paloma, all the Spanish songs. And the two violinists now would play in harmony, primarily thirds, up and down the scale. All right, you're getting there, so as soon as they start playing in harmony, you're getting that package, swing, forte, and arrangement, that style. Then they found out they could add the guitar, amplified guitar by now. In the age of swing, amplified guitar came in, and the hillbilly bands as well. It hadn't been there before. But as soon as he started amplifying the guitar, then he has another voice to add to the violins. So you have three-part harmony. And then a band of good musicians can figure out, well, let's add a fourth part, and then you're on your way by then. And so we used to, the old opera snowboys, would get something like South Rampart Street Parade and fix it up in four-part harmony, and we could do the same thing Crosby can do with his instruments. There, we'd four go right on and play the same arrangement, and did.
Were you using written arrangements at this time?

Well, the violinist would write his arrangement and teach the rest of ours by ear, and we'd catch, the most complicated arrangements we'd catch instantly. Strange, how quickly we'd catch on to sometimes the most elaborate head arrangements.
Were these, were these musicians able to read music for the most part?
The two violinists could.
Who were they?

Kenneth Pitts and Cecil Brower. Cecil Brower is now in Nashville the leading, oh, hillbilly violinist, I suppose, of the whole country now. He's on most of the records than anybody at all. Cecil Brower.
Hmm.

Very famous. Kenneth Pitts and stayed in Fort Worth. And now this was with, with the Doe Boys. Doe Boys, yes. Those two were going to school at TCU studying. Both of them finally then got their BAs and they played, oh, the Bach Two Violet Concerto and kept telling the teacher about the piano player they had out there and what he was doing and all and one time arranged for me to go out and meet Keith Mixon kind of on an audition and that was a turning point in my life then. When I finally met the piano teacher, I'd been taking a few night courses but not in music. I couldn't read and didn't know anything and the fellow one time wanted to sing Liebestrom on the program and got an old classical, the Red Seal Victor records and had me go home and learn the thing off the record to play the same accompaniment that was on this record while he sang old Liebestrom. Of all things, why I don't know. Parker Wilson, he was a strange man.
Tell me something about him.

Well, he had the idea that since we were the Doe Boys and sold flour and traveled all over the country, we ought to have more prestige than just playing the hillbilly band and also the fort man, the whole, the mores there in Fort Worth and Dallas, the countryside was to look down upon the hillbilly musicians as being inferior. I don't know why but we would go to the Blackstone Hotel to play our program and go through the Salon where the violins were playing some kind of sweet music and we would think we were not up to their standards or they would think we weren't and this is somehow the reason why we were된 stuff with stuff with stuff with stuff with

we had to show our music was good and we had we were it was our music this was our we were dedicated to our own field and this was our banner and we held it up highly as we just flying as brilliantly as we could and in our holding this up we're holding up by the same token Scott Joplin and Kau Kau and all these people who went up there with us and have always been you see that's been our banner then
